clue.text: Polish in Ulster, rioting

indicators.note: people rioting are in disorder, so the letters of the place name are thrown out of order

blocks.note: the province's name, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A Pole caught up in riots in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like a nationality, but it is the noun meaning shine; Ulster is Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustre is a gloss or sheen on a surface, the same thing as a polish.

clue.text: Old gay criminal and prima donna in a romantic comedy film

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the two preceding words are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter as anagram material
a prima donna is a leading opera singer, a diva

explanation.surface: An elderly crook and a temperamental star appear together in a romcom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the anagrammed part to DIVA. Lady Godiva is a 2008 British romantic comedy named after the legendary naked rider of Coventry.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Godiva is the title of a 2008 British romantic comedy movie, so it is an example of such a film.

clue.text: Bypass small pack of hounds

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
a hunt is the body of hounds and riders that hunts together

explanation.surface: A little band of hounds takes a detour around something.
explanation.definitionFit: To shunt something is to divert it onto a side track, moving it out of the main way, as a bypass does.

clue.text: Lettuce and eggs chief's brought in

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: roe is the mass of eggs in a fish
main means chief or principal

explanation.surface: A cook gathers lettuce and eggs as the head chef arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 's here stands for 'is': chief is brought into the eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Romaine is the long-leaved variety of lettuce also called cos.

clue.text: Hint from a close friend

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to suggest indirectly
second meaning: a noun, a confidant

explanation.surface: Someone receives a tip from a trusted pal.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: the verb ends 'mate', the noun ends 'mit'.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to suggest something indirectly, and an intimate is a very dear companion.

clue.text: Novel PM distributes inside

indicators.note: inside places the giving-out phrase within the statesman's name

blocks.note: Lord North was British Prime Minister from 1770 to 1782
to distribute is to hand out, here in the third person

explanation.surface: A prime minister sharing out a new policy within the party.
explanation.walkthrough: HANDS OUT goes between the last two letters of NORTH. 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: North and South is Elizabeth Gaskell's 1855 novel set in an industrial town.

clue.text: People in uniform

blocks.note: taken as written
a habit is the distinctive dress of a monk or nun

explanation.surface: Folk dressed in uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People' looks like a plural noun but is the verb: to people a place is to fill it with inhabitants.
explanation.definitionFit: To people a region is to occupy and live in it, which is what inhabit means.

clue.text: Every other substitute

blocks.note: first meaning: an adjective, every second one
second meaning: a noun, a stand-in or reserve

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a phrase about replacing things; the word is both an adjective for every second one and a noun for a deputy.
explanation.definitionFit: Alternate days are every second day, and an alternate is a deputy who can take someone's place.

clue.text: Italian novelist must collect hard copy

indicators.note: to collect something is to take it in, so the novelist's name gathers a letter inside

blocks.note: Umberto Eco wrote The Name of the Rose
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: An Italian author has to fetch a hardback edition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard copy' looks like a printout, but hard gives a single letter and copy is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo repeats a sound, so it is a copy or imitation of it.

clue.text: Leader of band in flat, the elder of two brothers

blocks.note: drum is old British slang for a home or flat
in British public schools the elder of two brothers is called major, the younger minor

explanation.surface: A bandleader shares a flat with his older brother.
explanation.walkthrough: Drum for a dwelling is thieves' slang; major and minor distinguish brothers at the same British boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: A drum major marches at the head of a military or marching band, leading it.

clue.text: Old golf club taking two years to get to grips with fire-raiser's mischief

indicators.note: getting to grips with something means grasping it, so the pair of letters holds the next piece between them

blocks.note: a jigger was an old iron-headed golf club
Y is the abbreviation for year, twice
a poker stirs up, or raises, a fire

explanation.surface: An antique club and two years of arson suggest some underhand mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fire-raiser' suggests an arsonist; it is the iron rod for stirring a fire. The two Ys grip it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jiggery-pokery is informal British for trickery or underhand dealing, a kind of mischief.

clue.text: Couple strike small child

blocks.note: to hit is to strike
CH is the abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: Two people strike a little child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' looks like a pair of people but is the verb, to join.
explanation.definitionFit: To hitch a trailer to a car is to couple or fasten them together.

clue.text: Being hissed at shopping for a goose?

blocks.note: first meaning: an idiom for a performer being jeered by an audience
second meaning, taken literally: fetching the poultry for dinner

explanation.walkthrough: Geese hiss, which ties the two halves together; the question mark flags the literal second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To get the bird is British slang for being booed or hissed by an audience, from the hissing of geese.

clue.text: Top actor not quite becoming top author

indicators.note: not quite means falling just short, so the final letter of the actor's name is dropped

blocks.note: best means top or supreme
Peter Sellers, the comic actor of the Pink Panther films

explanation.surface: A leading actor almost turns into a leading writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bestseller can be a writer whose books sell in huge numbers, so a top author commercially.

clue.text: Parking within remove exhaust

indicators.note: within places the single letter inside the following word

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
to delete is to remove

explanation.surface: Instructions to take an exhaust off a parked car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exhaust' suggests a car's tailpipe; it is the verb meaning use up.
explanation.definitionFit: To deplete a supply is to use it up, to exhaust it.

clue.text: One despicable person in photo, a Latin practising robbery on the high seas

definitions.text: practising robbery on the high seas

indicators.note: in places the first two pieces inside the word for a snapshot

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a rat is a contemptible person
pic is short for picture
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A villain appears in a photograph with a Latin American engaged in piracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'despicable person' is a familiar crossword term for a rodent; the photo word is split so the first two pieces sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Piratical describes a pirate, someone who robs ships at sea.

clue.text: Legal action brought against head, a fruitcake

blocks.note: nut is slang for the head
a case is a lawsuit

explanation.surface: Someone sues a boss who is clearly a lunatic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought against' places the lawsuit after, so up against, the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruitcake and nutcase are both informal words for an eccentric or crazy person.

clue.text: Collection in class

blocks.note: first meaning: an assortment of different things
second meaning: a kind or sort

explanation.surface: Money gathered in a school class.
explanation.definitionFit: A variety is an assortment of mixed items, and also a sort or category within a species.

clue.text: Continuing too long, and with no purpose?

blocks.note: first meaning: seemingly never stopping
second meaning, read cryptically: lacking an aim or goal

explanation.walkthrough: An end is a purpose, so something end-less literally has none; the question mark flags this playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Endless describes something that seems to go on forever, and split up it means lacking any aim.

clue.text: Conductor in rear of bus taking silver

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its tail end, so only its final letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
argent is the heraldic word for silver

explanation.surface: A bus conductor at the back of the vehicle collects silver coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests a bus ticket collector; it is Sir Malcolm Sargent, the orchestral conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Malcolm Sargent was a celebrated English orchestral conductor, long associated with the Proms.

clue.text: Film of artist, US portrait painter

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician
Henry Inman was a 19th-century American portrait painter

explanation.surface: A documentary about an American portrait artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain Man is the 1988 Oscar-winning film starring Dustin Hoffman and Tom Cruise.

clue.text: Incautious deed worried those present at a TV recording?

definitions.text: those present at a TV recording?

indicators.note: worried means agitated or troubled, so the letters before it are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: both words, letter for letter, are the fodder

explanation.surface: A rash act troubled the people watching a show being filmed.
explanation.definitionFit: A studio audience is the crowd invited to watch a television programme being recorded.

clue.text: Regular turned up with bandaged right cheek

indicators.note: something bandaged is wrapped round, so the first word encloses the letter
in a down clue, turned up means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: even means regular or uniform
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A soldier in the regulars shows up with a dressing on his right cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheek' looks like part of the face; it is the definition meaning audacity.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerve and cheek both mean impudent boldness or audacity.

clue.text: Cold shoulder and rolls served up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: buns are bread rolls

explanation.surface: A cold joint of shoulder served up with bread rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold shoulder' looks like a dish to go with the rolls; it is the verb meaning to ignore.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the cold shoulder is to ignore them deliberately, to rebuff them.

clue.text: Specialist area in hospital in French resort

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the town's name

blocks.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital
Nice is a resort on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: A specialist department in a hospital on the Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a specialised corner of a market or field, a specialist area.

clue.text: Passing maple here that's rotten

indicators.note: something rotten has decayed and fallen apart, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: both words, letter for letter, are the fodder

explanation.surface: Walking by a maple tree that has decayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' looks like walking past; it is the adjective meaning transient.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemeral means lasting only a short time, as a passing fancy does.

clue.text: Sweet shot may hit this window

blocks.note: first meaning: a round striped peppermint boiled sweet
a shot aims at the centre of a target
third meaning: a thick round pane, or a small circular window

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: the British humbug-like sweet, the centre of a target that a shot may hit, and a small round window. The surface suggests a stray shot breaking a window.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull's-eye is a peppermint boiled sweet, the centre of a target, and a circular window or bulging pane.

clue.text: Ready to drive off, wearing harness

blocks.note: dressed in something means wearing it
gear can mean harness, the equipment of a working animal

explanation.surface: A coachman in harness, about to set off.
explanation.definitionFit: A car in gear has its transmission engaged, so it is ready to move away.
